nodes.label: Ashot I and Smbat I
nodes.full: Ashot I, crowned king of Armenia in 884 with recognition from the caliph al-Mu'tamid and the Byzantine emperor Basil I, built a kingdom in Shirak and Ayrarat; his son Smbat I the Martyr (890–914) kept it through wars with the Sajid emirs of Azerbaijan, until he was captured and put to death by Yusuf ibn Abi'l-Saj in 914.
nodes.src: John Draskhanakertsi, History of Armenia 16–23; Thomas Artsruni, History of the House of the Artsrunik 3; Nina Garsoïan in R. Hovannisian (ed.), The Armenian People, vol. 1 (1997).

nodes.label: Ashot II and Abas I
nodes.full: Ashot II 'the Iron', son of Smbat I, regained the throne with Byzantine and Abbasid backing and in 922 was confirmed by the caliph as 'king of kings' (shahanshah); Abas I (928–953) was a peaceful king who made Kars his seat and built its cathedral and walls. The period was one of recovery after the Sajid wars.
nodes.src: John Draskhanakertsi 41–55; Stepanos Taronetsi, Universal History 3.1; Garsoïan 1997.

nodes.label: Ashot III to Gagik I
nodes.full: Ashot III 'the Merciful' (953–977) moved the royal seat to Ani in 961 and built its first walls; Smbat II (977–989) enlarged them and Gagik I (989–1020), who built the cathedral of Ani, led the kingdom at its height with a population and wealth which the Armenians remembered as a golden age.
nodes.src: Stepanos Taronetsi 3.46–3.48; Aristakes Lastivertsi, History; Garsoïan 1997.

nodes.label: Hovhannes-Smbat and Gagik II
nodes.full: Gagik I's sons, Hovhannes-Smbat (1020–1041) and Ashot IV, fought over the realm, Hovhannes bequeathing his part to Basil II's Byzantium and the war of succession was ended by the young Gagik II (1042–1045), who was lured to Constantinople, where he gave up the kingdom to the emperor Constantine IX; Ani was occupied in 1045.
nodes.src: Aristakes Lastivertsi, History 9–14; Matthew of Edessa, Chronicle; Garsoïan 1997.

nodes.label: Kings of Vaspurakan
nodes.full: Gagik Artsruni (908–943), made king of Vaspurakan by the caliph and the Bagratid Smbat I, built the island palace and church of Aghtamar in Lake Van; his successors ruled until Senekerim-Hovhannes gave the kingdom to Basil II in 1021–1022 in return for lands in Sebasteia, taking his people west.
nodes.src: Thomas Artsruni, History of the House of the Artsrunik; Aristakes 6; Garsoïan 1997.

nodes.label: Kars, Lori and Syunik
nodes.full: Alongside the central kingdom smaller Armenian kingdoms arose: Kars (963), under a branch of the Bagratids, the Kingdom of Tashir–Dzoraget (Lori) under the Kiurikians (979), and Syunik, under its Siwnid kings in the south, each with its own church patronage and court. They divided Armenia between local rulers.
nodes.src: Stepanos Taronetsi; Aristakes; Matthew of Edessa; Garsoïan 1997.

nodes.label: David III of Tao
nodes.full: David III, kouropalates of Tao, built up the south-western Georgian principality, defended it against Arab and Byzantine neighbours, built the cathedral of Oshki (963–973), helped Basil II against the rebel Bardas Skleros in 979 and, after supporting the rebellion of Bardas Phokas in 987, had to promise the emperor his lands after his death in 1000. He was the central figure of the Georgian polity of his time.
nodes.src: Kartlis Tskhovreba; Aristakes; Stephen Rapp, Georgian Christian Identity (2003); Cyril Toumanoff, Studies in Christian Caucasian History (1963).

nodes.label: Bagrat III
nodes.full: Bagrat III, of the Bagrationi house and through his mother heir to the Abkhaz kings, succeeded to the Abkhaz kingdom in about 978 and, on the death of his father Gurgen in 1008, to Kartli, and so united western and eastern Georgia in one realm with its capital at Kutaisi. He is the first king of a united Georgia.
nodes.src: Kartlis Tskhovreba; Sumbat Davitis-dze, Chronicle of the Bagrationi; Toumanoff 1963; Rapp 2003.

nodes.label: George I and Bagrat IV
nodes.full: George I (1014–1027) fought Basil II over Tao, lost the war in 1022 and gave up the lands; his son Bagrat IV (1027–1072), a boy when he came to the throne, held the kingdom against his Georgian magnates and the Byzantines, and from the 1060s faced the Seljuks, who raided Georgia in 1064 and 1068 and exacted tribute.
nodes.src: Kartlis Tskhovreba; Rapp 2003.

nodes.label: Sajids
nodes.full: The Sajids, a dynasty of Soghdian origin (Muhammad ibn Abi'l-Saj, 889–901, and his brother Yusuf, 901–928), governed Azerbaijan, Arran and for a time Armenia for the caliph, and fought the Bagratids; their main towns were Maragha, Ardabil and Barda, and they were displaced by the Daylamite Salarids.
nodes.src: Al-Tabari; Ibn Miskawayh, Tajarib al-umam; Minorsky, Studies in Caucasian History (1953).

nodes.label: Shaddadids
nodes.full: A Kurdish dynasty, the Shaddadids, took Dvin in 951 and ruled the lands between the Kura and Araxes, Ganja, Barda and Dvin, for more than two centuries, paying tribute to Seljuk lords after 1054 and recognising Georgia and Ani at intervals; Fadl I and Abu'l-Aswar Shavur ruled the principality at its height.
nodes.src: Minorsky, Studies in Caucasian History (1953); Minorsky, A History of Sharvan and Darband (1958).

nodes.label: Murder of Smbat I
nodes.full: In 914 Yusuf ibn Abi'l-Saj, who had held Smbat I captive in the fortress of Kapouyt Berd, had him tortured and crucified at Dvin, an act which the Armenian historians recorded as martyrdom and which made Smbat 'the Martyr'. The caliph was at the time unable to restrain his governor.
nodes.src: John Draskhanakertsi 33–35; Thomas Artsruni 3; Ibn Miskawayh.

nodes.label: Rus’ at Barda
nodes.full: A fleet of Rus' came down the Volga and across the Caspian in 943, took the town of Barda in Arran, held it for several months, and were finally driven off by disease and the army of Marzuban ibn Muhammad. Ibn Miskawayh gives a detailed account of its markets and the invaders' behaviour.
nodes.src: Ibn Miskawayh, Tajarib al-umam (trans. in Minorsky, A History of Sharvan and Darband, 1958); Minorsky 1953.

nodes.label: Georgian–Byzantine war
nodes.full: When George I of Georgia tried to recover the lands of David III of Tao, which Basil II had claimed, the emperor invaded Georgia in 1021–1022, defeated the Georgian army at Svindax in 1022 and forced the king to give up Tao, Phasiane and other lands and his young son Bagrat as hostage.
nodes.src: Aristakes 1–4; Kartlis Tskhovreba; Rapp 2003.

nodes.label: Annexation of Vaspurakan
nodes.full: Under pressure from Turkmen raids and his brothers, Senekerim-Hovhannes of Vaspurakan gave the kingdom to Basil II in 1021–1022, and moved with his family and some 14,000 followers to Sebasteia, where he was made governor; the Byzantines set up a theme of Vaspurakan.
nodes.src: Aristakes 6; Matthew of Edessa; Garsoïan 1997.

nodes.label: Surrender of Ani
nodes.full: In 1044 Constantine IX demanded Ani as a legacy of Hovhannes-Smbat; the Armenian army under Vahram Pahlavuni held off the imperial forces and the Georgian king, but the archbishop Peter and the nobles gave the city to the Byzantines in 1045 and the king, Gagik II, was given lands in Cappadocia. Ani became the seat of a Byzantine doux.
nodes.src: Aristakes 14–18; Matthew of Edessa; Garsoïan 1997.

nodes.label: Fall of Ani
nodes.full: The Seljuk sultan Alp Arslan took Ani after a siege of twenty-five days on 16 August 1064; the Arab historian Sibt ibn al-Jawzi reports that the Turks killed its population and that corpses blocked the streets and the survivors were taken captive. Aristakes Lastivertsi, a contemporary Armenian, describes the carnage. The city was held by Seljuk governors and from 1072 by the Shaddadids.
nodes.src: Sibt ibn al-Jawzi, Mir'at al-zaman; Aristakes 24; Garsoïan 1997.

nodes.label: Turkmen raids
nodes.full: From the 1030s Oghuz and Turkmen horsemen under Seljuk lords began to raid Armenia, Georgia and Arran, attacking Vaspurakan in 1016 and then Georgia in 1049, Ani in 1048, Kars in 1054, and by the 1060s the whole region. The disunited kingdoms were unable to resist.
nodes.src: Aristakes; Matthew of Edessa; Claude Cahen, The Formation of Turkey (1968).

nodes.label: Two crowns
nodes.full: Ashot Bagratuni received in 884–885 a royal crown from the caliph al-Mu'tamid through his envoy and another from the Byzantine emperor Basil I, so that Armenia's king was made by both empires; the arrangement of a king under two overlords served the Bagratids' security.
nodes.src: John Draskhanakertsi 16–17; Thomas Artsruni 3.1; Garsoïan 1997.

nodes.label: Union of 1008
nodes.full: With the death of his adoptive father Gurgen of Kartli in 1008, Bagrat III took Kartli as well as Abkhazia, and was recognised as 'king of the Abkhazians and the Kartvelians'; the Georgian chronicle describes the unification of the Georgian-speaking lands under one crown, which would later rule Tbilisi, Kakheti and the south.
nodes.src: Kartlis Tskhovreba; Sumbat Davitis-dze; Rapp 2003.

nodes.label: Peace of 1022
nodes.full: After the battle of Svindax Basil II and George I made a treaty by which the emperor kept the province of Tao, Phasiane and Kola and took Bagrat IV as hostage, and in return George kept his kingdom; the lands were organised as the Byzantine themes of Iberia and Mesopotamia.
nodes.src: Aristakes 4; Kartlis Tskhovreba; Rapp 2003.

nodes.label: Byzantine themes
nodes.full: Byzantium made new frontier provinces in the east out of annexed lands, the themes of Taron (968), Iberia (1000/1023), Vaspurakan (1021) and Ani (1045), under military governors and with some Armenian and Georgian nobles retained in imperial service, with great estates given to them and heavy taxation.
nodes.src: Aristakes; Matthew of Edessa; Garsoïan 1997.

nodes.label: Shirakavan
nodes.full: In 862 the Catholicos Zacharias and the prince Ashot called a council at Shirakavan to reply to the Patriarch Photios's letter urging the Armenians to accept Chalcedon; the Armenians refused, declared their loyalty to their own church and to the Fathers of Nicaea and Ephesus, and cut off their relations with the Byzantine patriarch.
nodes.src: Letters of Photios and the Catholicos; John Draskhanakertsi 22; Garsoïan 1997.

nodes.label: Catholicosate at Ani
nodes.full: The Catholicos Vahan or Khachik I made the Armenian patriarchal see in Ani in 992 and built the cathedral of the Holy Mother of God in Ani as its church; the primate remained there until the fall of the city and subsequently followed the Armenians west.
nodes.src: Stepanos Taronetsi; Aristakes; Garsoïan 1997.

nodes.label: Iviron on Athos
nodes.full: John the Iberian, a Georgian noble of David III's circle, and his son Euthymius founded in 980–983 the monastery of Iviron on Athos with Byzantine imperial support; it became the greatest Georgian cultural centre abroad, with its scriptorium, translators and library. Georgians led the monastery for centuries.
nodes.src: Life of John and Euthymius (Giorgi Mtatsmindeli, 1042); Rapp 2003.

nodes.label: Albanian church fades
nodes.full: As Arabic sources increasingly name the lowlands 'Arran' and 'Shirvan' and Islam spread through the plains under Arab and Turkic emirs, the Albanian church and language declined; in the highlands of Karabakh and Gardman, among the Armenian-speaking princes, the Albanian catholicosate survived under the Armenian church and its see moved to Gandzasar later.
nodes.src: Movses Kaghankatvatsi; Minorsky 1953; Hewsen, Armenia: A Historical Atlas (2001).

nodes.label: Cathedral of Ani
nodes.full: The cathedral of Ani, begun under Smbat II in 989 and finished under Gagik I in 1001, was designed by the architect Trdat, who had restored the dome of Hagia Sophia after the earthquake of 989; a domed basilica of local tuff, with blind arcades and slender engaged columns, it is the masterpiece of Armenian medieval architecture and is in the Ani World Heritage site (2016).
nodes.src: Ani cathedral inscription; Stepanos Taronetsi 3.48; UNESCO World Heritage no. 1518 (2016).

nodes.label: Aghtamar
nodes.full: The church of the Holy Cross at Aghtamar, built for King Gagik of Vaspurakan by the architect-priest Manuel in 915–921, is covered outside with a frieze of reliefs of biblical scenes, Jonah, David and Goliath and the prophets, and hunting and fruit-bearing vines, the most complete figural sculpture of medieval Armenia.
nodes.src: Thomas Artsruni, History 3; Sirarpie Der Nersessian, Aght'amar: Church of the Holy Cross (1965).

nodes.label: Haghpat and Sanahin
nodes.full: The monasteries of Sanahin (966) and Haghpat (976–991), founded by Queen Khosrovanuysh, wife of Ashot III, and their Kiurikian successors, with churches, libraries, scriptoria and schools, are UNESCO-listed and show the monastic centres of the kingdom of Lori.
nodes.src: Haghpat and Sanahin inscriptions; UNESCO World Heritage no. 777 (1996).

nodes.label: Georgian cathedrals
nodes.full: In the age of David III and Bagrat III the Georgian lands saw the building of the great domed cross-in-square cathedrals of Oshki (963–973), Bagrati in Kutaisi (completed 1003) and Svetitskhoveli at Mtskheta (1010–1029), the last by the architect Arsukisdze. They are monuments of the united kingdom.
nodes.src: Cathedral inscriptions; UNESCO World Heritage nos. 708 (Mtskheta), 710 (Gelati; Bagrati was removed from the list in 2017); Rapp 2003.

nodes.label: Khachkar
nodes.full: The cross-stone or khachkar, a slab carved in relief with a cross on a field of vine, rosette and interlace, appears in Armenian lands from the ninth century, the earliest dated example being the stone of Queen Katranide at Garni of 879, and becomes the great form of Armenian funerary and votive art. UNESCO inscribed the tradition in 2010.
nodes.src: Garni khachkar of 879; UNESCO Representative List of Intangible Heritage (2010).

nodes.label: Etchmiadzin Gospel
nodes.full: The Gospel copied in 989 by the scribe Hovhannes, later bound in ivory plates of the sixth century and now at the Matenadaran, with miniatures of the evangelists and the Fountain of Life, is one of the earliest dated Armenian illuminated books of the Bagratid time.
nodes.src: Etchmiadzin Gospel (Matenadaran MS 2374); Der Nersessian 1977.

nodes.label: Narekatsi
nodes.full: Grigor of Narek, a monk and the greatest poet of medieval Armenia, wrote at the monastery of Narek in Vaspurakan the Book of Lamentations (Matyan voghbergutyan), 95 prayers in an intense, personal poetry, completed about 1002; the Armenian church honours him as a Doctor of the Church (2015).
nodes.src: Grigor Narekatsi, Book of Lamentations (trans. T. Samuelian, 2001); Papal declaration (12 April 2015).

nodes.label: Historians of the Bagratids
nodes.full: John Draskhanakertsi, the Catholicos, wrote the History of Armenia about 925; Thomas Artsruni's History of the House of the Artsrunik (c. 904 and 10th c.) tells of Vaspurakan; Stepanos Taronetsi of Taron (c. 1004) wrote a Universal History; and Aristakes Lastivertsi, an eyewitness of the fall of Ani, wrote a history of the years 1000–1071.
nodes.src: John Draskhanakertsi, History of Armenia (trans. K. Maksoudian, 1987); Thomas Artsruni (trans. R. Thomson, 1985); Aristakes (trans. R. Bedrosian, 1985).

nodes.label: Translators of Iviron
nodes.full: Euthymius the Athonite (955–1028) and Giorgi the Athonite (1009–1065) translated from Greek into Georgian large parts of the Bible, the Fathers, hagiography and liturgy, and revised the Georgian literary language; the Iviron library became a repository of Georgian manuscripts.
nodes.src: Giorgi Mtatsmindeli, Life of John and Euthymius; Rapp 2003.

nodes.label: Georgian chronicle and hymnbook
nodes.full: Giorgi Merchule wrote the Life of Grigol Khandzteli in 951, Sumbat Davitis-dze wrote the Chronicle of the Bagrationi about 1030, and the hymnographer Mikael Modrekili compiled in 978–988 the Iadgari, a hymnbook; together they establish a literary culture in Georgian.
nodes.src: Giorgi Merchule 951; Sumbat Davitis-dze; Iadgari of Mikael Modrekili (978–988); Rapp 2003.

nodes.label: Wealth of Ani
nodes.full: Ani, on the roads from Trebizond to Persia and from Georgia to Syria, grew to a city of perhaps 100,000 people (estimates range up to 200,000) with merchants' quarters, tax on caravans, workshops and royal revenues; Byzantine, Persian and Arab goods passed through it, and the number of its churches, some say a thousand and one, became proverbial.
nodes.src: Aristakes; Matthew of Edessa; excavations (N. Marr, 1892–1917; Ani Archaeological Site, 1990s–).

nodes.label: Markets of Barda and Dvin
nodes.full: Arab geographers describe Barda as a great market town, with fruit, silk and horses, a mosque and a Friday market, and Dvin for its fine cloth and dyes. Ibn Hawqal and al-Muqaddasi note the markets of Arran and the Armenian dye, and the Rus' raid shows the wealth of Barda.
nodes.src: Ibn Hawqal, Surat al-ard; Al-Muqaddasi; Ibn Miskawayh.

nodes.label: Vineyards and orchards
nodes.full: The Georgian and Armenian lands of the age were supported by the intensive farming of terraces, vineyards, orchards and grain in the river valleys, supplemented by mountain pastures; wine was made in great quantity for church and market, and the monasteries held much land and labour.
nodes.src: Rapp 2003; Garsoïan 1997.

nodes.label: Walls of Ani
nodes.full: Ashot III's walls of 961 and Smbat II's double rampart of 989, with towers, sited on the neck of the triangle between two ravines, made Ani one of the best defended cities of the East. Their remains, with the later Kiurikian additions, stand today.
nodes.src: Smbat II inscriptions; Stepanos Taronetsi; Ani excavations.

nodes.label: Trdat and the pointed arch
nodes.full: Trdat's cathedral at Ani and his work at Hagia Sophia are cited by some scholars as an early use of the pointed arch and clustered piers of the kind later found in Western Gothic building, a claim which others question. His design for the Constantinople dome of 989 is attested by Stepanos Taronetsi.
nodes.src: Stepanos Taronetsi 3.48; Der Nersessian 1977; Garsoïan 1997.

nodes.label: Armenians go west
nodes.full: After the annexations the Armenian elite and many of the people moved to Byzantine lands, Senekerim's followers to Sebasteia, Gagik II and his house to Cappadocia and Cilicia, and Armenian soldiers and colonists to Syria, Melitene and Edessa; the migration prepared the Armenian principalities in the Taurus.
nodes.src: Aristakes; Matthew of Edessa; Garsoïan 1997.

nodes.label: Byzantine titles and gifts
nodes.full: Byzantium kept the Caucasian princes within its system by honorary titles, magister, curopalates, patrikios and doux, annual payments and marriages, as the Emperor Constantine VII's treatise 'On the Administration of the Empire' (c. 950) describes in a long chapter on the princes of Armenia and Iberia.
nodes.src: Constantine Porphyrogenitus, De administrando imperio 43–46; Garsoïan 1997.

nodes.label: Dvin earthquake
nodes.full: An earthquake on 28 December 893 destroyed Dvin, the capital of the caliph's province and a great trading city, with large loss of life: Arab and Armenian chroniclers give figures running from tens of thousands upwards. It was one of the worst catastrophes of the period in the Caucasus.
nodes.src: Thomas Artsruni 3; Al-Tabari; John Draskhanakertsi 25.

nodes.label: Coming of the Turks
nodes.full: In the eleventh century the Seljuks and their Oghuz followers moved from Central Asia into the Iranian plateau, Armenia and Anatolia, and the Bagratid kingdoms, which had won their independence in a time of Abbasid weakness, fell between Byzantium's annexations and the Turkish conquest.
nodes.src: Cahen 1968; Garsoïan 1997.

nodes.label: Queen Khosrovanuysh
nodes.full: Khosrovanuysh, queen of Ashot III and mother of kings, founded the monasteries of Sanahin and Haghpat and is named in their inscriptions as their patron, one of a number of royal women who patronised church building in the kingdom.
nodes.src: Haghpat and Sanahin inscriptions; Garsoïan 1997.

nodes.label: Captives of Ani
nodes.full: Sibt ibn al-Jawzi writes that the Seljuk troops killed the people of Ani so that nobody could count the dead, and that the streets were blocked with corpses; Aristakes mentions the survivors, the men taken as slaves and women into households. The numbers are rhetorical.
nodes.src: Sibt ibn al-Jawzi; Aristakes 24.

nodes.label: The villager
nodes.full: Most of the people were peasants, shinakan, who worked estates of the nobility, the church and the king under dues in kind and service, with a lower class of dependants; the inscriptions on monastery walls record gifts of villages with their population from the lords.
nodes.src: Monastery inscriptions of Haghpat, Sanahin and Horomos; Garsoïan 1997.

nodes.label: Ashot Bagratuni and the Arab province
nodes.full: Ashot Bagratuni became prince of princes in 862 and in the later ninth century the Caliphate’s power in Arminiya declined; the Bagratids rose from the Arab province to a kingdom.
nodes.src: background — see the Arab Caucasus folio (caucasus-645-884)
